title: {{NAME}} and the Valley Where Old Magic Lives
moral: The oldest things and the newest things understand each other better than anyone expects.

pages.content:
The valley appeared on no geological survey and no satellite image, which was not because it was hidden but because the instruments that looked for it simply slid past without finding anything, the way your eyes skip over things that exist in a register slightly outside the ordinary. {{NAME}} found it because he had been collecting fossils on the ridge above and rolled an ammonite down the slope by accident. He climbed down after it.

The valley floor was lush and dense and ran warm with a mist that smelled of pine resin and old rain. Through the mist, something enormous moved with the slow, settled confidence of a creature that has lived here since the word 'here' was first invented. A diplodocus. Then another. Three more behind them, their necks arcing above the canopy like living bridges.

And between the diplodocus, moving through their legs with a serenity that suggested this was entirely ordinary, three unicorns. Their coats were the deep silver of new moonlight and their horns caught what light filtered through the mist and distributed it like prisms. The diplodocus regarded them with the mild, warm affection of creatures that have shared a valley for a very long time.

pages.content:
The closest unicorn noticed {{NAME}} first. She was the smallest of the three, with a horn that split the mist around her as she turned her head, scattering tiny rainbows across the ferns. Her eyes were the deep violet of dusk after rain, and she trotted toward him in the direct, curious way of animals who have never needed to be afraid of anything and therefore never learned how.

Her name was Prism, a name {{NAME}} felt certain of within about thirty seconds of meeting her, with the instinctive naming certainty he had always possessed. She put her nose to the ammonite in his hand and her nostrils flared. Then she looked at the braided strap on his wrist where another ammonite was attached and made a sound of delighted recognition.

One of the diplodocus swung its long neck in a slow arc to look at {{NAME}} from above. He was very far away from the ground, that diplodocus, and {{NAME}}'s neck ached pleasantly from looking up at her. She blinked at him with eyes that were patient and clear and so deep they seemed to contain more than the valley.

{{NAME}}'s face was wide open with wonder, a smile he could not have suppressed if he tried.

pages.content:
The situation requiring attention, {{NAME}} gradually understood through observation rather than any verbal explanation, was a young diplodocus named Rum who had managed to get the tip of his tail wedged between two large boulders at the valley's western end. Not dangerously, but uncomfortably, and Rum had been trying to free himself for several hours with decreasing patience and increasing tail-wagging, which was making the problem worse and the other diplodocus increasingly concerned.

The other two unicorns were already there: a stallion named Shard with a horn like cut crystal and a mare named Lace whose mane moved in a wind that wasn't blowing for anything else. They were examining the boulders with their horns, tracing the stone's grain lines, and {{NAME}} realised with a jolt of recognition that they were looking for the fault points. The exact places to apply pressure.

Prism led him forward at a trot. {{NAME}} ran alongside her, pulled his fossil strap from his wrist, and used it to measure the gap between the boulders. Then he looked at Shard, pointed at one boulder, touched his shoulder to indicate pushing, and looked a question.

Shard's crystal horn dipped once. The three of them arranged themselves.

pages.content:
The boulder moved when all four of them pressed simultaneously, which was a matter of timing, and the timing was established by Prism who made a single clear resonant note at exactly the right moment.

Rum pulled his tail free with an undignified scramble and an enormous splash of tail-wagging relief that scattered mist in every direction and knocked {{NAME}} gently sideways into the ferns. He lay there looking up through the fern fronds at the valley sky, which was that deep impossible blue that happens only in hidden valleys, and laughed.

Above him, Rum's enormous face appeared over the fern-line, looking down at him with an expression that was unmistakably sheepish. Then all four diplodocus heads appeared, arranged in a row above the ferns, each one regarding {{NAME}} from a different height.

Prism walked over, stepped carefully over {{NAME}}'s legs, and stood between him and the diplodocus heads as if introducing two parties who were already quite capable of handling the introduction themselves. Shard made a sound. Lace echoed it. The oldest diplodocus answered with a sound that resonated in {{NAME}}'s ribcage like a cathedral bell.

It felt, somehow, like being welcomed.

pages.content:
The valley settled into evening slowly, the way places do when they have no particular reason to hurry. The diplodocus herd moved to the valley's lower end where a warm spring fed a wide, shallow pool, their feet moving with the unhurried rhythm of things that have done this for a very long time and expect to continue doing it.

Prism settled beside {{NAME}} in a clearing carpeted with ancient soft moss. Shard and Lace grazed nearby, their horns quiet now, the prism-scatter of their light dimming to a soft steady glow. Rum had his head in the pool and was making contented sounds.

{{NAME}} lay on his back in the moss and held the ammonite from his pocket up against the deepening sky, turning it in his fingers, its ancient spiral catching the unicorns' soft light.

A hundred and fifty million years old, this fossil. The valley around him ran older still. And Prism's warm flank against his side felt like the present moment, perfectly alive.

His eyes closed on their own, gradually and without argument.

Goodnight, finder of hidden valleys. Dream of deep time and silver light, and wonder what else this valley might hold.
